# Introduction and Data Description
New York City has the largest subway system in the United States, and it serves as an essential part of the city's public infrastructure. There are many benefits to widespread public transportation systems, but maximizing their effectiveness requires an understanding of how people use public transit in their everyday lives.

This exploration and analysis specifically examines New York City's subway ridership in Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Bronx, and Queens during the week of September 15-21, 2024. This specific week was chosen because we felt it was likely going to be the best representation of a relatively normal week, meaning there are no holidays, school is in session, and it is not off season.

Specifically, we proposed the following three questions: “How do NYC subway ridership volumes vary throughout the day?”, "Which hours have the highest ridership average (weekdays vs. weekends)?", and "Do these hours correspond to commuting periods?"

```{r Read in packages and data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ezids)
library(car)
project <- read.csv("~/Desktop/Fall 2026/DATS6101/DATS6101_Project_MTA_Subway_Hourly_Ridership.csv")
```

```{r Data Cleaning}
# Make sure columns are cast to correct types
project$borough <- as.factor(project$borough)
project$payment_method <- as.factor(project$payment_method)
project$fare_class_category <- as.factor(project$fare_class_category)
project$ridership <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", project$ridership))
project$transfers <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", project$transfers))

# Checking for any NA values
colSums(is.na(project))

# Checking for duplicates 
sum(duplicated(project))

str(project)

# Checking for any negative values to make sure there were no stragglers in the data cleaning 
sum(project$ridership < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(project$transfers < 0, na.rm = TRUE)


# Add 24-hour time column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    timestamp = mdy_hms(transit_timestamp),
    hour = hour(timestamp)
  )

# Add categories for morning, afternoon, evening, night
# Morning (5am - 10:59am), afternoon (11am - 3:59pm), evening (4pm - 8:59pm), night (9pm - 4:59am)
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    time_of_day = case_when(
      hour >= 5 & hour < 11 ~ "Morning",
      hour >= 11 & hour < 16 ~ "Mid Day",
      hour >= 16 & hour < 21 ~ "Evening",
      TRUE ~ "Night"
    )
  )

# Add day of week column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    day_of_week = wday(timestamp, label = TRUE)
  )

# Weekend vs. Weekday column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(day_type = if_else(day_of_week %in% c("Sat", "Sun"), "Weekend", "Weekday"))

# Commuter hours column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    commute_type = case_when(
      day_type == "Weekday" & hour >= 5 & hour < 11 ~ "Morning Commute",
      day_type == "Weekday" & hour >= 16 & hour < 21 ~ "Evening Commute",
      TRUE ~ "Other Hours"
    )
  )

project$time_of_day <- as.factor(project$time_of_day)
project$day_of_week <- as.factor(project$day_of_week)
project$day_type <- as.factor(project$day_type)
project$commute_type <- as.factor(project$commute_type)
```

For the data cleaning portion, we first converted all the variables to either numeric or factor. We also checked for any NA values as well as duplicates. There were none for either of these, which ordinarily could have been suspicious, however considering that this data was cleaned by the MTA prior to having been uploaded for public downloads, we interpreted this more as a testament to the MTA's strengths.

# Analysis and Interpretation

**Overview**

In order to further analyze the three questions of interest, four different statistical tests were performed on our dataset. These tests consisted of a two-sample t-test comparing mean hourly ridership in commute versus non-commute periods, a two-sample t-test comparing mean hourly ridership between weekdays and weekends, a one-way ANOVA that compares mean hourly ridership between different time-of-day categories (morning, midday, evening, and night), and a one-way ANOVA that compares mean daily ridership between the four boroughs in the dataset.

**Commute vs. Non-Commute t-test**

A two-sample t test was conducted to determine if there was a statistically significant difference between the mean hourly ridership during commute and non-commute periods. Commute periods were classified to be during the morning or evening, which falls between 5-11am and 4-9pm in the context of this dataset. Non-commute periods were classified as midday and night periods, falling from 11am-4pm and 9pm-5am. 

The null hypothesis for this test states that the mean hourly ridership during commute periods is equal to the mean hourly ridership during non-commute periods. The alternative hypothesis states that the mean hourly ridership during commute periods is different from the mean hourly ridership during non-commute periods. Before conducting this test, the assumptions were checked. We found that the population standard deviation was unknown given that we took a sample of the data and that the sample size is large enough per the central limit theorem to be robust against a normality violation. The independent observation may be violated due to our data being a time series set, but we continued with the two-sample t-test because it most closely fit the situation we are analyzing.

```{r Commute vs. Non-Commute t-test}
hourly_ridership <- project %>%
  mutate(commute_period = if_else(commute_type %in% c("Morning Commute", "Evening Commute"), "Commute","Non-Commute")) %>%
  group_by(timestamp, day_type, time_of_day, commute_period) %>%
  summarize(total_ridership = sum(ridership, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Commute"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Commute"])
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Non-Commute"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Non-Commute"])

# t-test for commute time vs. non-commute time means
commute_period_test <- t.test(total_ridership ~ commute_period, data = hourly_ridership)
commute_period_test
```

At the $\alpha$ = 0.05 level, this test produced a T statistic equal to 8.7228 with 84.945 degrees of freedom. The associated p-value was very small (1.975e-13). Given these findings, there is sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. We are able to conclude that there is a statistically significant difference between the mean hourly ridership in the commute periods versus the non-commute periods.

A further look at the t.test output showed that the mean hourly ridership in the commute group was 250,605 and the mean hourly ridership between the non-commute group was 104,204.5. Additionally, we are 95% confident that the the difference in the mean hourly ridership between the commute and non-commute groups is between 113,029.8 and 179,204.5.

**Weekday vs. Weekend t-test**
```{r Weekday vs. Weekend t-test}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekday"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekday"])
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekend"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekend"])

# t-test for weekday vs. weekend means
weekday_weekend_test <- t.test(total_ridership ~ day_type, data = hourly_ridership)
weekday_weekend_test
```

**ANOVA: Differences in mean hourly ridership between time-of-day categories**
```{r Time-of-Day ANOVA}
# Assumptions check
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (time_category in unique(hourly_ridership$time_of_day)) {
  x <- hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$time_of_day == time_category]
  qqnorm(x, main = paste("Q-Q Plot:", time_category))
  qqline(x)
}

leveneTest(total_ridership ~ time_of_day, data = hourly_ridership)

# One way ANOVA test and post hoc
time_anova <- aov(total_ridership ~ time_of_day, data = hourly_ridership)
summary(time_anova)

time_post_hoc <- TukeyHSD(time_anova)
time_post_hoc
```

**ANOVA: Differences in mean daily ridership between boroughs**
```{r Borough ANOVA}
# Daily ridership total for each borough
borough_daily <- project %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(timestamp)) %>%
  group_by(date, borough) %>%
  summarize(total_ridership = sum(ridership, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Assumptions check
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (b in unique(borough_daily$borough)) {
  x <- borough_daily$total_ridership[borough_daily$borough == b]
  qqnorm(x, main = paste("Q-Q Plot:", b))
  qqline(x)
}

leveneTest(total_ridership ~ borough, data = borough_daily)

# One way ANOVA test: Do daily averages in each borough differ?
borough_anova <- aov(total_ridership ~ borough, data = borough_daily)
summary(borough_anova)

# Post hoc tests
borough_post_hoc <- TukeyHSD(borough_anova)
borough_post_hoc
```
